mentions.quote: having bathed the blessed Vāsudeva with clarified butter, having worshipped him with perfumes, flowers, incense, lamps, food offerings
having fasted and worshipped the blessed Vāsudeva with unhusked rice grains

he should meditate on the blessed Vāsudeva, wearing a diadem, earrings, and armlets, with the Śrīvatsa mark, his chest adorned with a forest-garland, of gentle form, with four arms, holding a conch, discus, mace, and lotus, with the Earth goddess between his feet
meditate on the puruṣa, Vishnu, the twenty-fifth principle, who is without qualities
O Vāsudeva. O primeval god. O god of love. O protector of love. O protector of the earth.
her feet held by the god of gods, Vishnu

entities.description: The supreme deity of the text, presented as the cosmic puruṣa, object of meditation, and lord of all beings addressed by a litany of divine epithets.
entities.justification: Vishnu is the central divine figure across chapters 90–99, serving as the supreme cosmic principle, object of ritual worship, and the meditator's ultimate goal.

mentions.quote: Seeing Śrī, blazing with austerity, her feet held by the god of gods, Vishnu, her lovely color like refined gold
Thus addressed, Lakṣmī then spoke to the Earth, standing before the foremost of gods: 'I ever stand, O you of golden color, at the side of the god Madhusūdana.'
mentions.role: speaker explaining her cosmic dwelling places

entities.description: The goddess of fortune and prosperity, consort of Vishnu, who describes the auspicious places where she dwells in the cosmos.
entities.justification: Lakṣmī (Śrī) is an active narrative figure in chapter 99 who enumerates her dwelling places across the cosmos in response to Earth's question.

mentions.quote: This body, O Vasudhā, is called the field (kṣetra)
Having been thus addressed, Vasumatī (the Earth) made a salutation with her knees and head and said
the Earth goddess, delighted, asked the goddess

entities.description: The Earth goddess who receives cosmological teaching from Vishnu and then questions Lakṣmī about her divine dwelling places.
entities.justification: Vasudhā/Vasumatī serves as the interlocutor in the narrative frame of chapters 96–99, receiving teaching and conversing with both Vishnu and Lakṣmī.

mentions.quote: The month of Kārttika belongs to the deity Agni.
And Agni is the mouth of all the gods.
mentions.role: cosmic mediator between humans and gods

mentions.quote: By the gift of gold, fellowship with Agni.

entities.description: The fire deity who presides over the month of Kārttika and serves as the mouth of all the gods, the ritual mediator through whom oblations reach the divine realm.
entities.justification: Agni is named explicitly in chapter 89 as the presiding deity of Kārttika and the mouth of all gods, making him a theologically significant figure in the ritual logic of purification.

mentions.quote: The maker of a pond is eternally satisfied and enjoys the world of Varuṇa.
mentions.role: deity whose realm is attained through merit

entities.description: The Vedic deity of waters whose heavenly realm is the reward for constructing ponds as acts of public benefit.
entities.justification: Varuṇa is explicitly named in chapter 91 as the deity whose world is attained by one who builds water reservoirs.

mentions.quote: O Kapila. O teacher of Sāṃkhya.
mentions.role: epithet of Vishnu identifying him with the Sāṃkhya tradition

entities.description: The legendary sage-founder of the Sāṃkhya philosophical school, here invoked as an epithet of Vishnu in the litany of chapter 98.
entities.justification: Kapila is named among Vishnu's epithets in chapter 98, connecting Vishnu to the Sāṃkhya philosophical tradition.

mentions.quote: You are Sleep, the foremost of the world, Fortune, Firmness, Prosperity, Cessation, and Victory, Beauty, Radiance, Fame, and also Splendor, Sarasvatī, Speech, and the Purifier

entities.description: The goddess of speech and learning, invoked as one of the cosmic aspects or forms of Lakṣmī in the Earth's hymn.
entities.justification: Sarasvatī is explicitly listed in the Earth's praise of Lakṣmī in chapter 99, as one of the divine qualities or identities she embodies.

mentions.quote: By making it variegated, he attains the world of the Gandharvas.
mentions.role: celestial beings whose realm is a meritorious reward

entities.description: The celestial musician-beings whose heavenly realm is attained as a reward for beautifying a temple with colorful decoration.
entities.justification: The Gandharvas' world is cited in chapter 91 as the specific heavenly destination earned by adorning a temple with variegated colors.

mentions.quote: By giving clarified butter to Brāhmaṇas every day for the entire month of Āśvina, and having pleased the Aśvins, he becomes endowed with beauty.
mentions.role: twin deities pleased by ritual observance

entities.description: The twin divine physicians of Vedic mythology, pleased by daily offerings of clarified butter during the month of Āśvina, bestowing beauty on the devotee.
entities.justification: The Aśvins are explicitly named in chapter 90 as the deities gratified by month-long clarified-butter offerings, linking ritual practice to divine reward.

mentions.quote: The giver of a hundred cows, the worlds of Brahma.
mentions.role: deity whose realm is the highest reward for gift-giving

mentions.quote: O friend of Brahman. O you who love Brahman.
mentions.role: quality attributed to Vishnu in hymn

entities.description: The creator deity whose world represents the highest heavenly destination for the most generous givers of cows.
entities.justification: Brahma's world is the pinnacle of the gift-hierarchy in chapter 92, attained by giving one hundred cows, marking it as the supreme cosmic reward.

mentions.quote: having made a kṛṣṇājina (black antelope skin) with its hooves and horns, with golden horns, silver hooves, and adorned with a tail of pearls
He who gives a kṛṣṇājina, with its hooves and horns, Covered with sesame seeds and garments, adorned with all gems
mentions.role: meritorious gift equal to giving the earth

entities.description: A black antelope skin adorned with golden horns, silver hooves, and a pearl tail — the central ritual object of chapter 87, whose gift on the Vaiśākha full moon is said to equal giving the entire earth.
entities.justification: The kṛṣṇājina is the subject of the entire gift-ritual described in chapter 87, including a supporting verse that quantifies its cosmic merit.

surface_names: cup made of a Palāśa leaf

mentions.quote: From a cup made of a Palāśa leaf, from his hand, or from a potsherd.
mentions.role: vessel for eating in the forest-dweller stage

entities.description: The Palāśa (Butea monosperma) tree leaf used to fashion a simple eating cup for the forest-dweller (vānaprastha), emblematic of renunciation of household comforts.
entities.justification: The Palāśa leaf cup is explicitly prescribed in chapter 94 as one of the three acceptable eating vessels for a forest-dweller.

mentions.quote: O Vaikuṇṭha.

entities.description: The celestial abode of Vishnu, here used as a divine epithet in the litany of Vishnu's names recited by the Earth goddess.
entities.justification: Vaikuṇṭha appears in chapter 98 as one of Vishnu's epithets, referring both to his transcendent realm and his identity as its lord.

mentions.quote: when the moon is in the Revatī constellation, by feeding Brāhmaṇas with rice-pudding mixed with honey and clarified butter as a supreme food offering for the pleasure of Revatī, and having pleased Revatī, he becomes endowed with beauty.
mentions.role: lunar deity pleased by specific food offerings

entities.description: A lunar deity associated with the Revatī nakṣatra whose pleasure is invoked monthly by feeding Brāhmaṇas with rice-pudding, honey, and clarified butter.
entities.justification: Revatī is explicitly named in chapter 90 as a deity whose pleasure produces the boon of beauty, linking the lunar constellation to a personal divine presence.

mentions.quote: having satisfied seven Brāhmaṇas with sesame seeds mixed with honey, and having pleased the King of Dharma, he is purified from his sins.
By bathing in a river on every fourteenth day and worshipping the King of Dharma, he is purified from all sins.

entities.description: The deity of righteousness and death (Yama), the King of Dharma, who is propitiated through ritual bathing and feeding of Brāhmaṇas to achieve purification from sin.
entities.justification: The King of Dharma is named twice in chapter 90 as a deity whose pleasure directly results in the ritual practitioner's purification from sin.

themes.topic: Dana (gift-giving) as a primary path to spiritual merit and cosmic reward

mentions.quote: The gift of safety is superior to all gifts.
By him the four-cornered earth, with its oceans, caves, mountains, forests, and woods, Is given; there is no doubt in this.
Whatever is most cherished in the world, and whatever is beloved in the house, That very thing should be given to a worthy person by one who desires what is imperishable.

themes.justification: Chapters 87–93 are almost entirely structured as a typology of gifts and their corresponding heavenly rewards, making dāna the dominant theme of this window.

themes.topic: Ritual calendar: merit accrues from observances aligned with specific lunar months and constellations

mentions.quote: on the full moon day of Vaiśākha, having made a kṛṣṇājina with its hooves and horns
On the fifteenth day of the bright fortnight of Mārgaśīrṣa, when it is conjoined with the Mṛgaśiras constellation
If the full moon of Kārttika is conjoined with the Kṛttikā constellation, on that day, by giving a white bull

themes.justification: Chapter 90 is an extended catalogue of twelve months each paired with a specific nakṣatra and a corresponding ritual act, demonstrating that the timing of religious acts within the lunar calendar is determinative of their fruit.

themes.topic: Āśrama system: the four life-stages as a graduated path of spiritual discipline

mentions.quote: When a householder sees wrinkles and grey hair, he should take refuge in the forest.
A vānaprastha shall emaciate his body with austerity (tapas).
having been purified of his passions in the three stages of life, having performed the Prājāpatya sacrifice and given his entire wealth as a sacrificial fee, he shall become a renunciant.

themes.justification: Chapters 94–96 systematically describe the householder's transition to forest-dweller and then to renunciant, constituting the text's treatment of the final two āśramas.

themes.topic: Tapas (austerity) as the foundational cosmic and soteriological principle

mentions.quote: This entire world of gods and men has austerity (tapas) as its root, Austerity as its middle, and austerity as its end; and by austerity it is thus supported.
What is hard to practice, what is hard to obtain, what is distant, and what is difficult to do, All that is achievable by austerity (tapas); for austerity is indeed insurmountable.

themes.justification: Chapter 95 closes with a verse declaring tapas the root, middle, and end of the entire cosmos, elevating it from a personal practice to a metaphysical principle.

themes.topic: Renunciation and detachment from the body as the path to liberation

mentions.quote: He should see the impermanence of the world. The impure nature of the body. The distortion of form by old age.
Thus, in this ever-flowing world, there is no happiness whatsoever. And whatever is called happiness in relation to the absence of pain, that too is impermanent.
Therefore, having abandoned all that is perishable, he should meditate on the imperishable alone.

themes.justification: Chapter 96 presents an exhaustive analysis of the body's impurity and suffering as a systematic argument for renunciation, culminating in the injunction to meditate only on the imperishable.

themes.topic: Meditation (dhyāna) as a graduated practice from form to formless to Vishnu

mentions.quote: If he is unable to fix his attention on the formless, then having meditated on earth, water, fire, wind, ether, mind, intellect, self, the unmanifest, and the puruṣa, one after the other
he should meditate on the puruṣa like a lamp in the middle of the downward-facing lotus of his own heart
Whatever he meditates on, that he attains—this is the secret of meditation (dhyāna).

themes.justification: Chapter 97 presents a systematic hierarchy of meditation objects, from the gross elements up through Vishnu's iconic form, structured as a practical curriculum for yogins of varying capacities.

themes.topic: Kṣetra-kṣetrajña (field and knower of the field) as the framework for self-knowledge

mentions.quote: This body, O Vasudhā, is called the field (kṣetra); He who knows this, they who know that call him the knower of the field (kṣetrajña).
And know me also as the knower of the field (kṣetrajña) in all fields, O fair one; The knowledge of the field and the knower of the field is to be known always by one who desires liberation.
Thus the field (kṣetra), as well as knowledge and the object of knowledge, have been told in brief; My devotee, having understood this, becomes fit for my state of being.

themes.justification: Chapters 96–97 use the kṣetra-kṣetrajña distinction — drawn directly from Bhagavad Gītā chapter 13 — as the epistemological framework for liberation, making it a structuring theme of this section.

themes.topic: Brāhmaṇa as the supreme worthy recipient of gifts and ritual services

mentions.quote: he shall give it to a Brāhmaṇa who maintains the sacred fire, who has been adorned and covered with a pair of garments
To one who has mastered the Veda, infinite. But a priest is a worthy vessel for oneself alone.
One should not give even water to a twice-born man who follows the vow of a cat, Nor to a sinful man who follows the vow of a heron

themes.justification: Chapters 87–93 consistently direct gifts to Brāhmaṇas as the primary recipients, and chapter 93 explicitly ranks recipients by their learning, making Brāhmaṇa status the central variable in the gift-economy.

themes.topic: The cosmos as pervaded by Lakṣmī/Śrī — auspicious presence in all pure and virtuous things

mentions.quote: I dwell in the sun and in the moon, and in the sky adorned with hosts of stars
In one who abides in truth, who is devoted to the welfare of beings, who is endowed with forgiveness, and who is free from anger
In those who are mindful of dharma and endowed with compassion, I ever stand, and in Madhusūdana.

themes.justification: Chapter 99 is entirely structured as Lakṣmī's enumeration of her cosmic dwelling places, presenting Śrī as omnipresent in all that is ritually pure, morally virtuous, and cosmically ordered.

themes.topic: Sāṃkhya metaphysics: the puruṣa as the twenty-fifth principle beyond the twenty-four evolutes

mentions.quote: he should meditate on that which is beyond the twenty-four principles. Eternal, beyond the senses, without qualities, beyond sound, touch, form, taste, and smell
meditate on earth, water, fire, wind, ether, mind, intellect, self, the unmanifest, and the puruṣa, one after the other
meditate on the puruṣa, Vishnu, the twenty-fifth principle, who is without qualities

themes.justification: Chapter 97 employs the Sāṃkhya ontological framework of twenty-four principles plus the puruṣa as the scaffolding for its meditation hierarchy, implicitly drawing on that philosophical tradition without naming it directly as a source.

themes.topic: Public works (wells, tanks, bridges, temples) as meritorious acts creating long-term cosmic reward

mentions.quote: for the maker of a well, half of his evil deeds perish when water begins to flow in it
The maker of a bridge attains heaven.
The maker of a temple attains the world of that very deity whose temple he makes.

themes.justification: Chapter 91 presents a catalogue of public meritorious works — wells, ponds, trees, bridges, and temples — each tied to a specific heavenly reward, framing civic infrastructure as a form of religious practice.

themes.topic: Hypocritical religiosity (baiḍālavratika / bakavrata) as a category deserving severe censure

mentions.quote: One who makes a banner of dharma, is ever greedy, deceitful, a hypocrite in public, Is to be known as a baiḍālavratika, violent, and a betrayer of all.
They fall into the Blinding Darkness hell because of that sinful deed.
He who, not being a religious ascetic, lives by the guise of one, He takes away the sin of the ascetics and is born in the womb of an animal.

themes.justification: Chapter 93 introduces specific named categories of hypocritical religious observance — the cat-vow and the heron-vow — and assigns them the harshest karmic consequences, making anti-hypocrisy a distinct ethical theme.
